brief.subject: Fake debt collectors halted, plus a $63 million pricing settlement
brief.headline: Court Freezes Phantom Debt Collectors; Family Dollar Settles Over Register Prices
brief.dek: A court halts debt collectors posing as lawyers, more states join a telehealth privacy suit, and two retailers settle pricing claims.
brief.lede: At the FTC's request, a federal court froze a debt collection operation accused of pressuring people to pay debts they often did not owe. If a caller demands payment for a debt you don't recognize, verify it before paying.

sections.heading: Phantom Debt Collectors Frozen
bullets: A federal court temporarily halted the operation and froze its assets after an FTC request.
Collectors allegedly posed as a law firm or claimed ties to attorneys to frighten people into paying.
They also allegedly threatened to contact victims' employers and relatives, a common pressure tactic.
Many targets reportedly did not owe the debts, so demand written proof before sending any money.

sections.heading: Telehealth Privacy Suit Expands
bullets: Five states joined the FTC's lawsuit against telehealth provider Hims and Hers in an amended complaint.
The suit alleges sensitive health data went to third-party advertising platforms despite privacy promises.
It also alleges users were misled about billing and cancellation, so check subscriptions and statements carefully.

sections.heading: Family Dollar Pays $63 Million
bullets: Family Dollar will pay $63 million to settle claims from the FTC and 17 States.
Shoppers were allegedly charged more at checkout than shelf tags, price labels and ads showed.
Compare your receipt against posted prices, especially on frequent small purchases.

sections.heading: Car Dealer's Low Prices Questioned
bullets: The FTC settled with Stream Auto Outlet, a Long Island, New York dealership group.
Regulators said advertised car prices were far below what buyers actually ended up paying.
Ask for the full out-the-door price in writing before committing to a vehicle.
